People imagine my job is translation. It is closer to demolition. I am given a sentence four countries have approved and asked whether it survives in three languages.
And when it does not survive, who decides what changes — you or the delegations?
I say what breaks. They decide what to do about it. Last month I flagged a phrase that was open to interpretation in two of the three, and it went back for another day.
Is the ambiguity ever deliberate? I have always assumed it is, and I have never had anybody in the room to ask.
Frequently. Ambiguity is sometimes the only thing everyone can sign. What I object to is a loophole nobody has noticed, which is a different animal entirely.
The accidental one. Because the deliberate one at least has an author who can be argued with.
Exactly. And there is a third kind, which is the sentence written so that no author exists at all. There has been a deterioration. By whom? The text will not say.
That is the one I find hardest to read honestly, because it is grammatical, it is polite, and it is doing something.
To take note of something is not to accept it.
The undertaking is real and the deadline is subject to a review.

Following the conclusion of this week's meetings, the parties reaffirm their commitment to the principles set out in the framework agreement. A comprehensive review of implementation has taken place, and there has been a marked improvement in cooperation since January. The parties take note of the report submitted by the smaller delegations and welcome its contribution to the discussion. An undertaking has been given with respect to the transfer of resources, subject to a further review, the timing of which will be determined in due course. The parties look forward to continued engagement in a spirit of good faith. That is the full text of the statement. There will be no questions this evening.

Off the record? We agreed the policy on the first afternoon. Everything after that was wording. Four days, and at the end of it we were stuck on one adverb, and three capitals had to approve the change. People laugh when I tell them that, and they should not, because the adverb decided whether the obligation had a date attached to it. Ambiguity gets a terrible press, and sometimes it is the only text everybody can sign, and a text everybody signs is worth more than a perfect text nobody signs. What I do regret is paragraph six. We gave an undertaking with no date, and I wrote part of it, and I knew at the time what we were doing. That one I would take back.
